prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification of topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect.

statement.case_for: Four of eight members placed B041 first and five placed it in the top three, and I think that reflects the substance. The Kane-Mele proposal and Z2 classification introduced band topology plus spin-orbit coupling as an organising principle for electronic matter. Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe experiment gave a direct transport fingerprint (quantised edge conductance) that made the idea a laboratory fact rather than a conjecture. The concept has since spread well beyond solids, into superconducting hybrid structures, photonics and topological protection ideas that matter for quantum information. Independent confirmation across many materials is more than fifteen years deep, the interpretation is stable, and recognition is if anything overdue. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the configuration most of the committee already converged on in the opening ballots (four of six proposers named exactly these three), and it gives a clean theory-theory-experiment attribution under the three-name limit.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely contested and the three-person limit forces uncomfortable omissions. Hasan's ARPES observation of three-dimensional topological insulators is a strong independent claim, and my configuration drops him; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp's group tested and are not among the credited names; Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy are central to the 3D theory. A prize framed on the quantum spin Hall effect risks looking like it under-credits the three-dimensional story, while a broader framing runs into the name limit. B029 and B041 are also overlapping claims on one compound discovery, so supporting both would split the vote for no scientific reason. Finally, the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize may be read by some as already having covered the field.

responses.point: Danielsson also ranks B041 first but would credit Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, dropping Mele in favour of the 3D materials work.
responses.response: I take the Hasan argument seriously, but I would keep Mele. The Z2 invariant and the graphene quantum spin Hall model are Kane and Mele's joint work, and the 3D classification by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore-Balents and Roy grows out of the same framework. Removing Mele while keeping Kane splits a single paper-level insight. Hasan's ARPES result is an experimental confirmation of a prediction already made by theory, whereas the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe was the first realisation of the topological state at all. If the committee wants a 3D component I would rather see it argued as a separate point than as a substitution for Mele, and I accept that this is a judgment call where reasonable members differ.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the topological entry first but through B029, crediting Kane, Molenkamp and Xue, so as to include the quantum anomalous Hall realisation.
responses.response: The quantum anomalous Hall effect is a real and beautiful experimental achievement, but I regard it as a later development inside the topological-insulator programme rather than part of its foundation, and Xue's work needs the earlier theory to make sense. Putting Xue in place of Mele leaves out one of the two originators of the classification. I would rather concentrate support on B041 than split it between B041 and B029, and I read Mehlig's first place as largely support for the same underlying topic, which would favour a single consolidated topological prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B041 only sixth, regards Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as plausible but contentious because Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan are omitted, and puts his first-place weight on the theta13 neutrino measurement.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is contentious, and I conceded the same in my own opening ballot; the name limit makes a prize here unavoidably imperfect. I do not think contention lowers the merit, since the Nobel committee has regularly awarded on a three-person subset of a larger community. Where I differ is on theta13: the discovery is clean, but credit sits with Daya Bay, RENO, Double Chooz and T2K collaborations, so the three-name configuration is at least as fragile on attribution as B041, and I did not rank it. I would ask him whether the attribution difficulty on B018 is any easier than on topological insulators.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first and places B041 third, regarding the topological credit as a compromise and the allocation as truly contested.
responses.response: I share her view that B041 is a compromise on credit, but I would stress that this is a difference in degree: B013 has a cleaner two-name attribution, and I regard it as a strong alternative. My reason for putting topological insulators ahead is breadth of scientific consequence, since the concept reorganised condensed-matter physics rather than delivering a better instrument. I would be content with B013 as a fall-back if the committee cannot settle the topological allocation, and I would not treat the precedent of the 2005 comb prize as a serious obstacle.

uncertainties: Whether Hasan or Mele takes the third theory/experiment slot, and how the committee weighs Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are outside the credited names.
Whether B041 and B029 should be treated as one topological discovery so that first-place support is not split.
My recollection of the 2D and 3D chronology is unverified.
Whether the committee sees the 2016 prize as having already covered topological matter.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041, B026 or B013 from the provided profile. For B046 (circuit QED) I have a field and institutional proximity: I work in circuit and waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and Chalmers hosted researchers linked to the 2025 prize, so I would consider recusal or at least caution if B046 were taken up.
